name: Picosecond laser (PicoSure/PicoWay)

card.summary: Ultra-short-pulse laser used for pigment, tattoos and acne scars; small prospective studies report scar improvement, with few large trials.
card.note: Clinic-performed; the main scar study was small, uncontrolled and limited to skin types III-IV.

quick.overview:
Picosecond lasers deliver energy in trillionths of a second. PicoSure and PicoWay are commercial devices of this type, used in clinics for tattoo and pigment treatment, skin texture and acne scars.

Published evidence for acne scars is limited to small prospective studies; a 2020 study of 18 completers reported improvement in scar grading scores after six sessions. Registered trials also cover wrinkles, melasma and skin tightening.
quick.mechanism: A fractionated picosecond laser creates tiny zones of injury in the epidermis. A microscopy study in one volunteer found micro-injuries concentrated in pigmented cells, with debris exfoliated over about four weeks, suggesting melanin as the main absorber of the beam.
quick.risks: The 2020 acne scar study concluded the treatment was safe in 18 patients with skin types III-IV, but no large safety dataset was identified, and pain was measured as an outcome. Results in other skin types are not covered. Treatments are performed in clinics.

lead: Picosecond lasers are lasers whose pulses last a trillionth of a second, shorter than the nanosecond pulses of earlier Q-switched devices. PicoSure and PicoWay are among the commercial systems clinics use for pigmented lesions, tattoos, skin texture and acne scars. For appearance, the payoff is a more even, smoother complexion: fewer dark spots and less visible scarring and pigment, produced by short in-clinic sessions [9][11].

The technology was developed first for tattoo removal, and a 2021 systematic review of 77 studies reported that its clinical indications have broadened to benign pigmented lesions, photodamage, melasma and scar revision [9]. Registered trials cover tattoos, melasma, wrinkles, skin quality and facial laxity [3][4][5][6][7][8].

For acne scars, a 2020 prospective study of a fractionated dual-wavelength picosecond laser reported improvement in physician-rated scar scores and patient-rated scores; the authors said few prospective studies of this device in acne scars had been published [1]. A 2017 imaging study described how fractionated non-ablative picosecond treatment injures skin on a microscopic level [2].
infobox: Acne scars, pigment, tattoos, wrinkles, laxity, photoaging

paras: Picosecond lasers deliver very high peak power in pulses shorter than nanosecond Q-switched lasers. A 2023 review notes that fitting a fractional optical delivery system, such as a diffractive lens array, produces an array of high-fluence microspots surrounded by low-fluence skin; this creates laser-induced optical breakdown in the epidermis and laser-induced cavitation in the dermis [11]. These small injuries are described as prompting skin regeneration and dermal remodeling [11].

Wavelengths differ by target. Studies in the loaded literature used 532 nm and 1,064 nm for acne scars [1], 755 nm alexandrite with a diffractive lens array for scars and photoaging [13][16], 730 nm titanium sapphire against 1,064 nm for nevus of Ota-like macules [15], and 730, 532 and 694 nm for freckles and solar lentigines [21].

In a 2017 study, a fractionated non-ablative picosecond laser was applied to the arm of one volunteer and imaged with multiphoton microscopy over four weeks. The study reported micro-injuries in the epidermis, damaged pigmented cells that suggested melanin as the main absorber for laser-induced optical breakdown, inflammatory cells near the injuries after 24 hours, and exfoliation of the injuries over four weeks. It was described as observational groundwork rather than evidence of clinical benefit [2].
Fractional picosecond treatment is described as encouraging skin regeneration and dermal remodeling after the laser-induced breakdown and cavitation events [11].

Beyond the 2020 acne-scar study [1], a prospective study evaluated a picosecond 755 nm alexandrite laser with diffractive lens array combined with radiofrequency microneedling for atrophic acne scars [13]. A randomized trial studied 1,064 nm fractional picosecond laser on postmastectomy scars in transgender men, treating one scar of each bilateral pair [14]. A 2024 review covers advances in laser therapies for scars generally [20].

A 2023 meta-analysis of six randomized trials found picosecond laser significantly reduced melasma severity scores, with high heterogeneity; the 1,064 nm subgroup showed significant reduction without notable side effects, while the 755 nm subgroup did not significantly improve scores compared with topical agents and caused post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation [10]. A 2025 split-face randomized study examined low-fluence 1,064 nm picosecond laser with and without micro-lens arrays for melasma [17], and a 2026 review covers lasers for melasma [19].

A systematic review of 41 trials of solar lentigine treatments reported success rates of 67.9% to 93.02% for picosecond laser, compared with ranges reported for other lasers and topicals [12]. A randomized trial compared 730, 532 and 694 nm lasers for freckles and solar lentigines [21].

The 2021 systematic review associated tattoo removal with level I evidence, rejuvenation and melasma with level II evidence and scar revision with level II-III evidence [9]. A 2023 review reports that fractional picosecond treatment has shown positive effects on photoaging, enlarged pores, dyspigmentation, wrinkles and atrophic scars, and says further research is needed [11]. A randomized split-face multicenter trial combined long-pulse 1,064 nm Nd:YAG with picosecond 755 nm alexandrite for photoaging [16]. A French-language review covers laser tattoo removal [18].

A prospective study enrolled 20 patients with skin types III-IV with acne scars; 18 completed six monthly sessions with both 532 nm and 1,064 nm fractionated handpieces. Physician-assessed scar grading scores fell from 15.22 to 10.61 for quantity and from 3.00 to 2.33 for quality, and patient visual analogue scores fell from 4.28 to 2.00, all reported as statistically significant. The authors concluded the approach was efficacious and safe, without a control group [1].

Registered trials include studies of picosecond lasers for tattoo removal with 60 participants (completed) [3], melasma with 40 participants (completed) [4], wrinkles using a specialised lens array in two 20-participant studies (completed) [5][6], skin quality [7], and facial skin tightening with a fractional 1,064 nm device [8]. The registry entries do not list results.

The 2021 systematic review identified 77 unique studies and concluded that picosecond laser is a safe and effective modality for a growing range of dermatologic conditions [9]. Further randomized and split-face trials listed above have addressed melasma, nevus of Ota-like macules, freckles, photoaging and postmastectomy scars [17][15][21][16][14].

The 2020 acne scar study concluded the treatment was safe in 18 patients with skin types III-IV and measured pain as an outcome [1]. In the melasma meta-analysis, the 755 nm subgroup was associated with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation [10]. The studies loaded do not report large safety datasets across all skin types; treatments are performed in clinics by trained operators [9][1].
The laser is categorised on the wiki under hardmaxx for scars and marks, alongside other in-clinic resurfacing options.

chain: Ultra-short laser pulses are fired at skin or pigment
Skin remodels and pigment is cleared by the body over weeks
More even tone and less visible scarring or marks
angle.text: Clinics use picosecond lasers to break up pigment and to stimulate skin renewal. People seek treatment for acne scars, sun spots, melasma and tattoos, with sessions spaced weeks apart.
